query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a fraction of the lower-melting-point element (e.g., vanadium) with a high‐melting‐point refractory element (e.g., tungsten) in a low-activation, BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: A low-activation refractory high-entropy alloy with a designed composition such as Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 that exhibits a single-phase BCC structure and moderate elevated-temperature strength (e.g., at ~873 K).
generation.intervention: Replace part of the vanadium content (e.g., around 50% of V atoms) with tungsten, without altering the overall phase stability, followed by a standard homogenization heat treatment to ensure chemical uniformity.
generation.conditions: Test at elevated temperatures (approximately 800–900 K) relevant to extreme high-temperature applications, such as those in nuclear or aerospace environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform single-phase BCC microstructure with fewer elemental segregations and enhanced solid-solution strengthening, due to the higher melting point and modulus of tungsten.
generation.mechanism: The inclusion of tungsten increases the alloy’s overall melting point and Young’s modulus, which enhances the resistance to dislocation motion (via improved edge dislocation pinning) and suppresses high-temperature softening, leading to a higher yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-modified HEA will show a measurable improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength relative to the baseline alloy, while maintaining acceptable ductility and phase stability at temperatures around 873 K.
generation.baseline: The original Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 HEA composition with vanadium as the lower-melting-point element.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under conditions where the temperature is high (around 800–900 K) and the alloy is used in extreme environments (e.g., nuclear reactor components or high-temperature aerospace applications).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal tungsten substitution level and any potential impacts on ductility and long-term phase stability require further investigation. There is also uncertainty in the quantitative extent of strength improvement until tested experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA samples: one with the baseline composition (Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2) and one where approximately 50% of the vanadium is replaced with tungsten. Subject both sets to identical homogenization heat treatments. Perform mechanical testing (e.g., compression or tensile tests) at elevated temperatures (~873 K) to measure yield strength and ductility. Use microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, XRD) to verify phase uniformity.
measurements: Phase stability and homogeneity via XRD/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength (or if they show significant loss in ductility or phase degradation) relative to the baseline samples under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In the process of pursuing high-performance materials, the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [] were introduced. The preeminent properties (such as high strength [,], good corrosion resistance [,,], fine tribological properties [,], remarkable softening resistance [,], and outstanding irradiation tolerance [,,,], etc.) enhance the application competitiveness of HEAs under extreme environments. Among them, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], which are characterized by a high melting point and prepared by methods such as vacuum arc melting, suspension melting, spark plasma sintering [], and wire electric discharge machining [], are expected to play a role in future high-temperature applications []. Compared with conventional alloys, HEAs, especially the body-centered cubic (BCC) structured ones composed of refractory elements, exhibit better irradiation tolerance for the extreme lattice distortions and chemical complexity, such as prominent resistance to hardening [,], suppressed dislocation evolution [,,], low volume swelling rate [,], and reduced radiation-induced segregation [,,], etc. Hence, the HEAs are considered to be a promising candidate for nuclear structural materials [,]

In this study, Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW RHEAs were designed for extremely high elevated-temperature strength by using the above guidelines: Ti and Zr of HfMoNbTaTiZr were replaced by W to increase the melting point and Young’s modulus. The proposed alloys will be compared with standard MoNbTaVW that contains vanadium instead of hafnium. Moreover, homogenization treatments at a temperature of 2100°C for 2 h, followed by air cooling, were conducted in an ultrahigh-temperature furnace in order to get the fully homogeneous state. Their microstructures and mechanical properties were investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and hardness and compression testing. The phase, temperature-dependent strength, and the ultrahigh elevated-temperature strength are discussed with the solution-strengthening mechanism, especially focusing on the contribution of edge-dislocation-induced strength.
